JUDICIAL DISSOLUTION OF A CALIFORNIA LLC — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Ventures, LLC

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — JUDICIAL DISSOLUTION OF A CALIFORNIA LLC INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme Ventures, LLC, a limited liability company organized under the laws of California, and describes Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03, part of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Corp. Code §§ 17701.01–17713.13). Section 17707.03 sets out the specific grounds on which a court may order the judicial dissolution of a California limited liability company, identifies who may bring that action, and provides a buyout mechanism the other members can use to avoid dissolution. It is prepared with reference to Jordan Lee's relationship to Acme Ventures, LLC. Statutory ground or grounds this information sheet may relate to, if known: management deadlock.

This information sheet is about court-ordered dissolution under § 17707.03 specifically. This project's existing LLC Dissolution and Cancellation document already covers the separate, non-judicial process of winding up and formally cancelling an LLC once dissolution has occurred by another route — for example, by vote of the members or an event specified in the operating agreement — including who conducts the winding up, the priority order for distributing remaining assets, and the certificate filings with the Secretary of State. This information sheet instead describes the distinct statutory grounds and procedure for asking a court to order dissolution in the first place, and the buyout alternative to that outcome, in depth that document does not.

This information sheet is educational only. It is not a verified complaint, does not itself commence any court proceeding, and does not determine whether any ground described below applies to Acme Ventures, LLC's circumstances, whether Jordan Lee has standing to bring such an action, or whether a court would order dissolution, the buyout alternative, or no relief at all in any specific case.

WHO MAY PETITION FOR JUDICIAL DISSOLUTION
Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(a) identifies who may bring an action asking a court to order a California limited liability company's dissolution: “any manager or…any member or members of a limited liability company.” The subdivision does not condition standing on holding any minimum percentage or number of membership interests, and does not distinguish between a manager-managed and a member-managed LLC in stating who may sue. The action is filed with “a court of competent jurisdiction,” which the subdivision's own text does not further define or confine to a particular county. Once such an action is filed on one of the grounds subdivision (b) specifies, subdivision (a) states that the court “may decree” the LLC's dissolution — phrasing that makes dissolution a discretionary remedy the court may order, not one that follows automatically from a ground being shown.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Pursuant to an action filed by any manager or by any member or members of a limited liability company, a court of competent jurisdiction may decree the dissolution of a limited liability company whenever any of the events specified in subdivision (b) occurs."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(a), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, standing to petition for judicial dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)

Code § 17707.03, and its lettered and numbered subdivisions (a) through (d) are not independent sources of corroboration for each other. This document does not address the separate, non-judicial dissolution and winding-up process — the events that trigger dissolution by vote or by the operating agreement's own terms, who conducts the winding up, the priority order for distributing remaining assets, and the certificate of dissolution and certificate of cancellation filings — which this project's existing LLC Dissolution and Cancellation document already covers. It also does not address any interim remedy, such as appointment of a receiver or provisional manager, that may or may not be available under other provisions of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, Title 2.6 of the Corporations Code, which are outside the scope of this document.

THE FIVE STATUTORY GROUNDS FOR JUDICIAL DISSOLUTION
Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(b) lists five events, any one of which lets a court decree an LLC's dissolution under an action filed as subdivision (a) describes. The first is that it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the LLC's business in conformity with its articles of organization or operating agreement. The second is that dissolution is reasonably necessary to protect the rights or interests of the complaining members — wording that does not, on its own text, require proof of any specific wrongdoing. The third is that the LLC's business has been abandoned. The fourth is that the LLC's management is deadlocked or subject to internal dissension. The fifth is that those in control of the LLC have been guilty of, or have knowingly countenanced, persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement, or abuse of authority. Subdivision (b) does not attach a separate minimum-ownership threshold to any of these five grounds, and its introductory text supplies no examples or illustrative list beyond the five numbered events themselves.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]

BUYOUT ALTERNATIVE TO DISSOLUTION — ELECTION AND VALUATION STANDARD
Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(1) gives the LLC's other members a way to stop a judicial dissolution suit without a dissolution being decreed: the statute lets them avoid dissolution “by purchasing for cash the membership interests owned by the members so initiating the proceeding, the ‘moving parties,’ at their fair market value.” Paragraph (1) also sets a damages rule tied to that buyout: if the moving party's initiation of the dissolution suit breached an agreement (the operating agreement is given as one example) with the purchasing party, resulting damages may be deducted from what the purchasing parties owe for the interests — except that no member who sues on the third, fourth, or fifth ground listed in subdivision (b) (business abandonment, management deadlock or internal dissension, or fraud, mismanagement, or abuse of authority) can be held liable for breach-of-contract damages for bringing that suit. If the purchasing parties elect to buy the moving parties' interests but cannot agree with them on fair market value, paragraph (2) requires the purchasing parties to post bond covering the moving parties' estimated reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, recoverable under paragraph (3); once that bond is posted, the court stays the winding-up and dissolution proceeding and itself proceeds to ascertain and fix the membership interests' fair market value.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "In any suit for judicial dissolution, the other members may avoid the dissolution of the limited liability company by purchasing for cash the membership interests owned by the members so initiating the proceeding, the “moving parties,” at their fair market value. In fixing the value, the amount of any damages resulting if the initiation of the dissolution is a breach by any moving party or parties of an agreement with the purchasing party or parties, including, without limitation, the operating agreement, may be deducted from the amount payable to the moving party or parties; provided, that no member who sues for dissolution on the grounds set forth in paragraph (3), (4), or (5) of subdivision (b) shall be liable for damages for breach of contract in bringing that action."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(1), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, buyout election to avoid judicial dissolution and the damages carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)
  "If the purchasing parties elect to purchase the membership interests owned by the moving parties, are unable to agree with the moving parties upon the fair market value of the membership interests, and give bond with sufficient security to pay the estimated reasonable expenses, including attorney’s fees, of the moving parties if the expenses are recoverable under paragraph (3), the court, upon application of the purchasing parties, either in the pending action or in a proceeding initiated in the superior court of the proper county by the purchasing parties, shall stay the winding up and dissolution proceeding and shall proceed to ascertain and fix the fair market value of the membership interests owned by the moving parties."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(2), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, bond and stay when the parties cannot agree on fair market value (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)

COURT-APPOINTED APPRAISERS, THE DECREE, AND PAYMENT CONSEQUENCES
Once a fair-market-value dispute over the moving parties' membership interests is before the court under Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(2), paragraph (3) directs the court to appoint three disinterested appraisers to appraise that value, referring the matter to them by court order that prescribes the time and manner for producing evidence if evidence is required. The appraisers' award, or the award of a majority of them, becomes final and conclusive on all parties once the court confirms it. The court then enters a decree that provides, in the alternative, for the LLC's winding up and dissolution unless payment for the membership interests is made within the time the decree specifies; if the purchasing parties fail to pay within that time, judgment is entered against them and against the surety or sureties on their bond for the moving parties' expenses, including attorney's fees. Paragraph (3) also gives any member aggrieved by the court's action the right to appeal. Paragraph (4) then addresses the reverse case — the purchasing parties timely paying to prevent dissolution: once the purchasing parties pay the moving parties the decreed value of their interests (or, on appeal, the value as fixed on appeal), and the moving parties receive that payment or its tender, the moving parties must transfer their membership interests to the purchasing parties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The court shall appoint three disinterested appraisers to appraise the fair market value of the membership interests owned by the moving parties, and shall make an order referring the matter to the appraisers so appointed for the purpose of ascertaining that value. The order shall prescribe the time and manner of producing evidence, if evidence is required. The award of the appraisers or a majority of them, when confirmed by the court, shall be final and conclusive upon all parties. The court shall enter a decree that shall provide in the alternative for winding up and dissolution of the limited liability company, unless payment is made for the membership interests within the time specified by the decree. If the purchasing parties do not make payment for the membership interests within the time specified, judgment shall be entered against them and the surety or sureties on the bond for the amount of the expenses, including attorney’s fees, of the moving parties. Any member aggrieved by the action of the court may appeal therefrom."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(3), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, court-appointed appraisers and the resulting decree (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)
  "If the purchasing parties desire to prevent the winding up and dissolution of the limited liability company, they shall pay to the moving parties the value of their membership interests ascertained and decreed within the time specified pursuant to this section, or, in the case of an appeal, as fixed on appeal. On receiving that payment or the tender of payment, the moving parties shall transfer their membership interests to the purchasing parties."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(4), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, payment and transfer once the purchasing parties pay to prevent dissolution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)

VALUATION DATE AND EFFECT OF A PLAINTIFF'S DISMISSAL
Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(5) fixes the default valuation date for the membership interests bought out under this section as “the date upon which the action for judicial dissolution was commenced,” while giving the court discretion to designate a different date on a party's motion and for good cause shown. Paragraph (6) addresses what happens if the manager, member, or members who filed the judicial dissolution suit later dismiss it: that dismissal does not affect the other members' rights to avoid dissolution under this section — meaning the buyout mechanism paragraphs (1) through (4) describe is not itself extinguished merely because the underlying suit was dismissed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "For the purposes of this section, the valuation date shall be the date upon which the action for judicial dissolution was commenced. However, the court may, upon the hearing of a motion by any party, and for good cause shown, designate some other date as the valuation date."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(5), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, default valuation date and the court's discretion to designate another (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)
  "A dismissal of any suit for judicial dissolution by a manager, member, or members shall not affect the other members’ rights to avoid dissolution pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(c)(6), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dismissal by the moving parties does not affect the other members' buyout rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17707.03.)

THIS SECTION DOES NOT LIMIT THE COURT'S OTHER REMEDIES
Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.03(d) is a savings clause: it states that nothing in the section is to be construed to limit the remedies otherwise available to a court of competent jurisdiction over the dissolution. On its own text, subdivision (d) does not itself identify what those other remedies are or where they are found; it only preserves them against an argument that § 17707.03's own grounds, standing rule, and buyout mechanism are the exclusive set of tools a court may use in a dissolution matter.

Paragraph (4) then addresses the reverse case — the purchasing parties timely paying to prevent dissolution: once the purchasing parties pay the moving parties the decreed value of their interests (or, on appeal, the value as fixed on appeal), and the moving parties receive that payment or its tender, the moving parties must transfer their membership interests to the purchasing parties.

citations.quote: The court shall appoint three disinterested appraisers to appraise the fair market value of the membership interests owned by the moving parties, and shall make an order referring the matter to the appraisers so appointed for the purpose of ascertaining that value. The order shall prescribe the time and manner of producing evidence, if evidence is required. The award of the appraisers or a majority of them, when confirmed by the court, shall be final and conclusive upon all parties. The court shall enter a decree that shall provide in the alternative for winding up and dissolution of the limited liability company, unless payment is made for the membership interests within the time specified by the decree. If the purchasing parties do not make payment for the membership interests within the time specified, judgment shall be entered against them and the surety or sureties on the bond for the amount of the expenses, including attorney’s fees, of the moving parties. Any member aggrieved by the action of the court may appeal therefrom.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, payment and transfer once the purchasing parties pay to prevent dissolution
citations.quote: If the purchasing parties desire to prevent the winding up and dissolution of the limited liability company, they shall pay to the moving parties the value of their membership interests ascertained and decreed within the time specified pursuant to this section, or, in the case of an appeal, as fixed on appeal. On receiving that payment or the tender of payment, the moving parties shall transfer their membership interests to the purchasing parties.
